intro: The parent reinterprets the children’s eyes as a light already preparing to leave. Mahler gives this sonnet a less regular musical shape than the first song, with chromatic links that repeatedly postpone a settled tonic.
question: How does the orchestra keep a phrase moving when the voice seems ready to come to rest?

sections.label: Opening argument · dark flames
sections.mNote: rising orchestral figures and an unsettled vocal line

sections.label: Central appeal · a brighter region
sections.mNote: the score opens into a contrasting D-major passage

cues.title: An unsettled beginning
cues.text: The orchestral opening starts with a rising cello phrase and gradually adds other lines. Across the song, listen for motion towards a resting chord that is diverted into another chromatic turn.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Song II, printed pp. 18–32; the opening cello line and chromatic continuation are score facts, not an identification of a chord from the audio.

cues.title: A sonnet about eyes
cues.text: Rückert’s poem has two four-line stanzas followed by two three-line stanzas: the shape of a Petrarchan sonnet. Its last image transforms the children’s eyes into stars visible on future nights.
cues.evidence: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-lied-2-nun-seh-ich-wohl-warum-so-dunkle-flammen/ The German text supplies the stanza pattern and final image; no modern English translation is quoted.

cues.title: Hear the inner movement
cues.text: Listen across the phrases for the strings and winds moving beneath a held vocal note. The singer need not change pitch for the harmony to change; the accompanying lines can shift the ground underneath it.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 18–25. This listening instruction concerns the song’s layered writing, not a timestamped inner-voice event.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Published after the premiere
cues.text: C. F. Kahnt publishes the cycle’s full score, orchestral parts and piano-vocal score in 1905, after the January premiere. Mahler’s songs therefore circulate in both orchestral and domestic forms from their first publication.
cues.evidence: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm Chronology records the August 1905 publications and the 29 January first performance.

cues.title: Contrast without a new world
cues.text: In the central part, compare the harp’s moving figures with the sustained wind and string lines. The score passes into D major, but the neighbouring-note motives still connect this brighter stretch with the opening.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 26–27. The report marks 2:26, then a rise around 2:40–2:45 before the quieter 3:00 window. The D-major region is identified from the score; its first chord is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The phrase withdraws
cues.text: A renewed swell gives way to a much quieter passage before the music gathers again. Compare the amount of space after that crest with the more continuous movement heard earlier.
cues.evidence: The recording’s analysis shows a drop from −8.0 dB at 2:45 to −26.4 dB at 3:00, then a rise at 3:05–3:15. No instrument or sung word is identified by those measurements.

cues.title: Return as recollection
cues.text: In the later part, listen for earlier melodic fragments rather than a complete repeated stanza. The orchestra can recall a vocal turn after the singer has moved on to different words.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 28–31 contain varied returns of earlier material. The exact first note of a returning motive is not timed here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A recording, not a premiere
cues.text: This performance was recorded on 20–21 June 1955 in Berlin’s Jesus-Christus-Kirche. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings with the Berlin Philharmonic under Rudolf Kempe; the Commons transfer comes from an EMI compact disc.
cues.evidence: Commons file description: File:Mahler - Kindertotenlieder, II (Fischer-Dieskau, Kempe, 1955).ogg. Session date and venue are corroborated by the Naxos 8.111300 back cover: https://cdn.naxos.com/SharedFiles/pdf/rear/8.111300r.pdf

cues.title: The orchestra completes the sentence
cues.text: The short postlude carries the music beyond the singer’s final phrase. Listen for its falling intensity and the time allowed for the remaining tones to disappear.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 32. The report marks 4:34; level falls from −21.4 dB at 4:35 to −46.6 dB at 4:50. The end of the sung line is not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Chromatic motion opens into a brighter region
transitions.how: The opening argument’s chromatic phrases give way to a more clearly defined D-major region in the written score. Harp figures move beneath sustained upper lines, with flutes lending the passage a different colour from the initial low-string phrase. The neighbouring-note motives remain: the contrast comes from their harmonic setting and spacing rather than from an unrelated tune.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 25–27. The 2:26 novelty peak precedes the 2:40–2:45 swell. The timestamp is provisional; written D major is not an audio-derived chord label.

transitions.title: Earlier phrases return without a full repeat
transitions.how: The brighter middle does not close off as an independent song. Its phrase subsides, and earlier melodic fragments reappear in voice and orchestra with different words and altered continuation. Mahler uses the instrumental lines to connect the fragments, so the return is heard as renewed argument rather than a restart of the whole opening.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed pp. 27–31. The 2:54 change leads into the very quiet 3:00 window, with renewed activity by 3:05. This does not align a particular word or melodic note.

transitions.title: The voice leaves the chromatic continuation
transitions.how: After the final vocal phrase, the orchestra continues the harmonic motion with falling lines and a short harp figure. The written close settles into C minor, but Mahler reaches it through chromatic voice-leading rather than a detached closing fanfare. The reduced texture and diminishing sound allow the postlude to finish the sentence begun by the voice.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, Sibley Music Library scan: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 Printed p. 32. The report’s strongest novelty peak is 4:34, followed by the final 4:35–4:50 decay. C minor comes from the written score, not the report’s inconsistent key estimates.

source.locator: Song II, printed pp. 18–32; passage-level scoring, not an instantaneous list of sounding parts. Timings are provisional score proportions checked against the recording’s level changes; no bar alignment or aural verification.

timeline.note: The cello line begins the orchestral prelude; other parts enter within the following bars.
Early vocal passage: strings and selected winds surround the singer with moving inner parts.
Central passage: harp figures run beneath the vocal line and sustained upper parts.
Earlier melodic material returns in a changing mixture of wind and string lines.
The closing instrumental passage passes between wind tones, strings and the harp’s final figure.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
